en.title: Doom Dev Slams Xbox: 'They Fundamentally Don't Understand Art' After Layoffs
en.summary: A lead programmer at id Software has voiced his deep frustration following recent layoffs, directly criticizing Xbox's management for what he perceives as a lack of artistic understanding and a detrimental impact on the studio's creative capabilities.
en.body:
The gaming world is still reeling from the significant layoffs that struck **id Software** in July, a studio synonymous with groundbreaking first-person shooters like **Doom** and **Doom Eternal**. Now, **Chris Hays**, a lead services programmer who has been with the studio since 2010, has broken his silence, delivering a scathing critique of **Xbox**'s parent company, **Microsoft**, and its understanding of game development as an art form.

Hays expressed his profound disappointment in a recent conversation, stating that the recent cuts, which saw 136 staff members let go, have fundamentally impacted the studio's ability to create the high-caliber AAA experiences fans have come to expect. "It's hard to make a game that is AAA, that's like we've done before, with half the people. And by hard, I mean impossible," Hays explained. He further elaborated on the devastating effect these layoffs have had on the studio's operational capacity. "It's hard to make a game when there are entire departments that are gutted that you need, entire disciplines that are gone." This directly contradicts the reassurances offered by id Software's management, which suggested the studio remains at a size comparable to when it developed the critically acclaimed **Doom (2016)** and possesses the necessary talent for future projects like **Doom: The Dark Ages**.

## The Human Cost of Corporate Restructuring

For Hays, the core issue lies in a fundamental disconnect between **Microsoft**'s business-centric approach and the human element that defines **id Software**. "We're half the same id. id was the people. What made us special was the people and the relationships we have," he lamented. This sentiment echoes a broader debate within the industry and among players about whether video games are truly considered art, and how corporate decisions can undermine the creative process. While some argue that games, with their narrative depth and intricate design, are indeed a form of art, others, like Hays, feel that executives making decisions from afar may not grasp the nuanced, collaborative effort required to realize such artistic visions. The sentiment that **Microsoft** and **Xbox** are attempting to downplay the internal unrest is palpable, as Hays pointed out that studio management is tasked with managing these sensitive communications.

## What This Means for Fans and the Future

The impact of these layoffs extends beyond the immediate employees. For fans who have followed **id Software**'s journey from its early days to its modern resurgence with the **Doom** franchise, this news is disheartening. The studio's ability to consistently deliver innovative and polished FPS experiences has been a cornerstone of the genre. The fear now is that the loss of experienced personnel and the potential disruption to established workflows could affect the quality and ambition of future titles. While **Doom: The Dark Ages** is slated for 2025, the internal turmoil at **id Software** raises questions about the long-term health and creative output of this legendary studio under **Xbox**'s stewardship.

## Looking Ahead

Fans will be closely watching for any further developments regarding **id Software**'s internal structure and the progress of **Doom: The Dark Ages**. The studio's ability to maintain its creative momentum despite these significant challenges will be a key indicator of its resilience and **Microsoft**'s commitment to preserving the unique identity of one of gaming's most iconic developers.

content_raw: After layoffs ripped through Doom developer id Software in July, lead services programmer Chris Hays has taken aim at Xbox: "They fundamentally don't understand art." Hays, who is currently employed at the studio behind first-person shooter classics like Doom Eternal and has been with the team since 2010, unloaded on the recent decision to cut 136 staff during a recent conversation with Andre Peschke on Auf ein Bier . He didn't mince words, to put it lightly. "It's hard to make a game that is AAA, that's like we've done before, with half the people. And by hard, I mean impossible," Hays said. "It's hard to make a game when there are entire departments that are gutted that you need, entire disciplines that are gone. "So, if they've got some kind of new plan for how this is going to work, that hasn't been told; we don't know what that is. The reassurances that we're still the same id and we're still going to do things, well, first of all, we're not the same id. We're half the same id. id was the people. What made us special was the people and the relationships we have." The "reassurances" Hays mentioned at least partially refer to some of the messages that have emerged in the fallout of last month's layoffs. id issued a statement to IGN July 10 that thanked fans for their support, acknowledging that, while the studio had been "impacted," the restructuring left it at "about the same size we were when making Doom 2016." It added, "We still have the crew we need to build the games and tech we're known for." id reclaimed its title as a leading FPS studio with its 2016 Doom game and went on to keep its crown with 2020's Doom Eternal and 2025's Doom: The Dark Ages . Hays said id's overseers at Microsoft and Xbox are trying to minimize the "unrest." "Studio management is given talking points on things that are allowed to be said and what is not allowed to be said," he added. "It feels like it is, instead, more reassurances. They don't want more people to jump ship and say, 'Oh, there's no more future in id, so we're all going to leave,' and then there's no one left. They don't want unrest. At the end of the day, most of it was just trying to tell us that, 'Oh, no, everything is fine. Things will be OK.'" Hays said the reality is that id now houses "less" than the number of staff that worked on Doom 2016. He noted that fans will certainly have their preferences in the series but added, "There is a lot more that went into each of the [Doom] games that went along. We made bigger and better games, but that's with twice as many people as we had. So, we have fewer than we had before. So, are we going to make something equivalent to a single-player Xbox 360 game? Because that's the size of the studio we have." id has a special place not only in gaming history but in the hearts of those who have continued to show up for the studio's work in the decades since its inception.
